prompt.context: A fast food chain recently bought a bovine meat-processing outlet to supply it with fresh hamburgers and other meats. The shop process is: cows enter from one end of the shop, meat gets processed in the middle, and then the meat gets packaged and delivered at the other end.
prompt.question: The manager of the butcher shop could not decide whether to have the cows walk or run into the meat processing room. Can you help him?

clarifying_info.q: What is processed at the shop?
clarifying_info.a: Only fresh hamburger meat is processed at the shop.

clarifying_info.q: How many hamburgers can be made from each cow?
clarifying_info.a: From each cow, you can make 20 hamburgers.

clarifying_info.q: How many hours per day and days per week is the shop open?
clarifying_info.a: The shop is open 10 hours per day, 5 days a week.

clarifying_info.q: How many cows can be processed per hour if cows walk?
clarifying_info.a: If cows walk in, 10 cows can be processed per hour given current labor.

clarifying_info.q: How many cows can be processed per hour if cows run?
clarifying_info.a: If cows run in, 25 cows can be processed per hour.

clarifying_info.q: How many outlets does the fast food chain have?
clarifying_info.a: The fast food chain has 10 outlets, and the meat-processing factory serves all 10.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population in the vicinity of each outlet?
clarifying_info.a: Each outlet serves a vicinity of about 30,000 people.

clarifying_info.q: How many competitors are there in each vicinity?
clarifying_info.a: There are about 3 other competitors in each vicinity, giving the chain a market share of about 25%.

framework: Understand shop capacity: calculate how many hamburgers can be processed per day/week when cows walk vs. run
Analyze cost implications: calculate total costs and cost per burger for each scenario
Estimate market size and demand: determine how many burgers per week the chain's outlets actually need
Match supply to demand: compare production capacity against actual demand and recommend accordingly

questions.prompt: Calculate the number of hamburgers produced per week if cows walk vs. run.
questions.guidance: Use the given throughput rates, hours per day, and days per week. Walking: 10 cows/hr x 10 hr/day x 5 days = 500 cows/week x 20 burgers/cow = 10,000 burgers/week. Running: 25 cows/hr x 10 hr/day x 5 days = 1,250 cows/week x 20 burgers/cow = 25,000 burgers/week.

math.setup: Burgers/week = cows/hour x hours/day x days/week x burgers/cow
steps: Walk: 10 cows/hr x 10 hr/day x 5 days/week = 500 cows/week
Run: 25 cows/hr x 10 hr/day x 5 days/week = 1,250 cows/week

questions.prompt: Calculate the cost per burger under each scenario using the cost table (Overhead: Walk $5,000 / Run $10,000; Labor: Walk $1,000 / Run $2,500).
questions.guidance: Total costs are $6,000 (walk) and $12,500 (run) per week. Divide by burgers per week to get cost per burger. Running reduces cost per burger by $0.10.

math.setup: Cost per burger = Total weekly cost / Burgers per week
math.answer: Walk: $0.60/burger; Run: $0.50/burger; running saves $0.10 per burger

questions.prompt: Estimate the weekly demand for burgers across all 10 outlets.
questions.guidance: Work top-down from total population served: 10 outlets x 30,000 people = 300,000 total population. 25% market share = 75,000 potential customers. 40% in target demographic = 30,000 desired customers. 1/3 will actually frequent the chain regularly = 10,000 active customers. Each visits twice a week = 20,000 visits. Half order a burger = 10,000 burgers/week.

math.setup: Apply successive filter rates to total addressable population
steps: Will frequent regularly (1/3): 30,000 x (1/3) = 10,000 active customers

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors might the manager consider when deciding between walking and running cows?

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Equipment wear and maintenance under higher throughput
Quality of meat (stress hormones from running cows may affect meat quality)

categories.name: Strategic
ideas: Future demand growth — could running capacity serve expansion?
Freshness and shelf life commitments to the fast food chain
Flexibility to handle demand spikes or seasonal variation

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Capital investment required to handle running cows at scale
Cost savings from lower cost per burger vs. risk of overproduction waste
Break-even analysis if demand grows toward 25,000 burgers/week

recommendation: Have the cows walk. Current weekly demand is 10,000 burgers, which exactly matches the walking-speed capacity of 10,000 burgers per week.
Although running reduces unit cost by $0.10 per burger, there is no current demand to justify producing 25,000 burgers per week — excess production would be wasted for a fresh product.
risks: If demand grows significantly, the walking scenario caps capacity at 10,000 burgers/week and could become a bottleneck
Meat freshness means there is no option to stockpile excess production — overproduction directly translates to waste and higher realized costs
next_steps: Monitor demand trends across the 10 outlets; if weekly burger demand approaches 10,000 units consistently, re-evaluate switching to running
Investigate whether meat quality (stress hormones) differs between walking and running cows before any change
Explore whether additional shifts could expand walking-speed capacity as a lower-risk alternative to running
